column1: What object does the book begin and end with?
column2: A rock — specifically, the silicon that becomes, across the whole chain, the substrate that now thinks and answers.

column1: What are the three parts of the book, as summarised in Chapter 42?
column2: Part I: how silicon is made. Part II: how silicon thinks. Part III: what happens when many thinking machines start talking.

column1: What is the loom metaphor in the chapter?
column2: A loom of cognition: biological and artificial minds are threads; the wire and protocols of Part III are the frame and shuttle; what they produce together — conversations, inferences, new sciences, new institutions — is the fabric.

column1: Who does the chapter say is in charge of the pattern on the loom?
column2: Nobody — vendors, regulators, engineers, and users are all weaving in different directions with different interests on the same loom.

column1: What does the chapter say it took to turn sand into a planet that can think about itself?
column2: Time, money, discipline, and a great many people who were good at their narrow task — no magic, no new physical law.

column1: How does the chapter characterise each step in the silicon-to-superintelligence chain?
column2: As ordinary engineering — each link was the next obvious thing to build, by people who could draw the diagram for the step after.

column1: What does the chapter say the book has not argued?
column2: That AI is good, that AI is bad, that superintelligence is imminent, or that it is impossible.

column1: What is the book's single argument, per the closing chapter?
column2: That the chain by which sand becomes thought is real, knowable, and made of ordinary parts — and anyone who wants to think clearly about the future has a right to see the chain whole.

column1: What does the chapter identify as the difference between a future that goes well and one that goes badly?
column2: The quality of attention paid by the people assembling it, and by the rest of us watching, while the assembly is still being done.

column1: How does the closing image describe the speed of the silicon's response?
column2: Answering billions of times a day in roughly the time it takes you to blink.
